The demo, mapped

Moon Faire, November 13, updated in the evening. All ten areas of the demo: what each place looks like, who is there, what can happen, how the places join, and where the fights are. Claude Fable 5.2 drafted it through your key from the lore notes, the approved plan and the fair folk. Everything is a draft for you to cut: each thing that can happen has a code (W2-c), so you can say "cut W2-c" or "change W4-a".

How to use this page
  • To approve the map: read the ten cards and tell me what to cut or change, by code.
  • All nine walking places are painted. Your eight new paintings (W2 to W9) are on their cards. Each one kept its guide closely: open "How the guide sits on your painting" on a card to see. Still to paint: only fight pictures, if you want your own for the fair, the crag and the lamp room.
  • Fights use your own moor clearing and four pictures borrowed from Envoi, as you chose. Two of the borrowed ones fit poorly; they are marked.
  • New on the evening of November 13: what you settled, story options from Opus 5.5 (does it have to be lamps?), and the two kinds of fight picture, shown side by side. They are the next three sections.
  • Names, people and lines are stand-ins, not lore. Drafting this page cost $11.20 on your key.

What you settled on November 13

  • All nine walking places are painted: Chris painted W2 to W9 on the evening of November 13, and each kept its guide closely.
  • Three rest spots: the party's own wagon in the fair square, the camp by the pool, and the airship at the landing ledge.
  • The sparring ring: the party fights wisps that keep drifting to the ring lamps.
  • Where a person's 3D model looks different from their note, the note changes. Three notes changed: the lamp-seller is no longer called old, the old lamplighter is an elderly woman, and the gate keeper is a man in a flat hat and waistcoat.
  • The story is open again: does it have to be lamps? Opus 5.5 laid out options (below).

Does it have to be lamps?

No. Claude Opus 5.5 (high effort, through your key) laid out 4 stories that fit the ten areas, the three foes and your lore. It was shown your nine paintings. They are options, not decisions: pick one, mix them, or throw them all out. Tell me by letter. None of them needs a painting redone.

How Opus reads the lamp story. The lamp story is clear. One thing is taken, there are twelve to win back, and the player sees the count fill on the hull. Your new paintings are built for it: empty brackets at W3, all twelve lit at W8. It is thin in three ways. Nobody knows why wisps take lamps. Once all twelve are home the captain's problem is solved, so the climb to the beacon has nothing at stake. And little of what is special about your world shows: not the moon, not the once-in-a-lifetime fair, not crystal power, not the four themselves.

A   Keep the lamps, give them a reason nothing to change

Wisps carry off the twelve lamps of the captain's airship. The four win them back on the moor. The captain flies them to the dead beacon, where the great wraith has been hoarding stolen light for years. The twelve lamps were only the newest she took. When she falls, all that light goes home.

At the fair
As drafted. Wisps drift into the fair after its lights, and the four see them off in the square and the stall row. At the mooring field they watch the last lit lamps lift off the hull and stream over the gate toward the moor. The captain says he won't fly her dark.
What you count in the wilds
Lamps. Each one comes back from a wilds fight where a wisp is seen holding a ship's lamp in its tendrils. In W4, W5 and W6 the set fight always has one. After that, walking fights each give one until that area's number is reached (3, then 4, then 5). Then walking fights there give none. Someone says each number out loud: the lamplighter's 'three, by my count' at W4, and the Ranger counting at W5 and W6. Each lamp won lights on the hull at W3. Zone 3 opens when all twelve are lit.
The great wraith
She sits in the cold cradle at the top of the beacon with every light she has taken since it died: lamps off passing ships, lanterns off the moor road, candles from windows. The flames in her ribs and the lanterns on her chain are those lights. The wisps fetch for her.
Why the four go
With the twelfth lamp lit, the captain says the wisps will be back for them tomorrow night, and for the fair's lamps after. The dead post at the Last Lantern shows she has done this before. The candles on the rug still lean toward the crag. The four go to end it.
The ending
The flames in her ribs and the lanterns on her chain come loose. They pour out through the broken arches as a stream of small warm lights going home across the moor in every direction. One goes back to the dead post at the Last Lantern. The beacon stays dark, as you painted it at W9. The last thing seen is the lit airship far out in the sky.
What it shows off
The captain and his airship, and the fair's lamps and lamplighter. Little of the moon, the four's own story, or crystal power.
Leans on
What the wraiths are: that the great wraith commands the wisps and takes light. The draft already assumes this, but it is yours to say.
Its weakest point
The last fight is not about the lamps any more, because they are already home. The climb runs on 'she'll do it again', and the four are doing an errand for a man they just met.
What would change in what is made
  • Counting rule written down as above, with the lamp shown in the wisp's tendrils
  • Each wild area's number said out loud by someone
  • Captain's line after the twelfth lamp: they'll be back for these, and the fair's next
  • F5 ending rewritten: the light streams home, the beacon stays dark
  • W9 and F5 lines: the ship is far out in the sky, as painted, not below

No painting needs redoing.

B   The beacon's broken crystal heart small to change

The dead beacon ran on solar crystal: a great crystal heart that drank the sun by day and shone all night for airships. It cracked long ago and its pieces lie scattered over the moor. The wisps carry them, drawn to the last bit of sunlight inside. The four gather the pieces and take the heart back up to its cradle.

At the fair
Wisps come into the fair after its warm lights. At the mooring field three wisps hang round the captain's ship. When they are beaten, one drops a sliver of crystal giving off a thin, steam-like shine. The captain knows it: beacon crystal, from the crag. Ships have flown wide of that crag ever since it went dark. He says: bring me the heart whole, and I'll lay her on the ledge so you can put it back.
What you count in the wilds
Pieces of the heart, won from wisps seen carrying a glowing piece. Same rule as A: the set fight in each wild area always has one, and walking fights give one each until the area's 3, 4 or 5. A small picture of the heart fills as pieces are won. Zone 3 opens when the heart is whole and starts to glow on its own.
The great wraith
She has made the cold cradle her nest. The light in her ribs is the sunlight that leaked out when the heart cracked. The lanterns on her chain are lights she took from ships that came too near the dark crag.
Why the four go
A whole heart is no use in a bag. It has to sit in the cradle, and she is sitting in it.
The ending
The heart is set in the cradle. Light rises from it like steam, up through the broken arches. A beam swings out over the moor and across the fair's glow, and the twelve lamps on the ship answer from below.
What it shows off
Crystal power that looks like steam, airships, why a beacon matters to people who fly, and the captain's world.
Leans on
How solar crystal power works and that beacons ran on it. Also what wisps are: things drawn to crystal light.
Its weakest point
'Collect the pieces' is the most familiar shape in games, and the four are hired hands again. It also makes the demo say how crystal power works, which you may want to keep for yourself.
What would change in what is made
  • The ship's-lamp prop becomes a glowing crystal piece a wisp carries
  • W3 opening scene rewritten: no lamps lift off the hull; a wisp drops a sliver of beacon crystal
  • The hull lamps lighting one by one goes, which saves work on the ship set piece; a small heart picture shows the count
  • The empty brackets at W3 are just the captain's lamps, stowed while moored; he hangs and lights all twelve to fly, which fits W8
  • F5: the cradle needs the whole heart set in it, and a rising light at the end
  • Great wraith: works as she is; you could change the glow colour to the crystal's light
  • Lines for the captain and the lamp-seller rewritten

No painting needs redoing.

C   The cold hearth calls every flame small to change Opus's pick

The crag beacon died long ago, and its fire went cold but never quite out. The great wraith is that fire: hungry, and calling every flame for miles to come and warm it. The wisps are flames that answered and went cold on the way, which is why they look so sad. Tonight the fair, the most light this moor has seen in a lifetime, is within reach of the call.

At the fair
At dusk the candles on the rug lean with no wind, as the singer already says. The lamplighter has gone out to hold the last lantern on the road because it keeps straining. Wisps drift into the fair after its lights. At the mooring field the captain has unhooked all twelve of his lamps and put them in a crate. 'They were pulling on their hooks. Toward the crag.' He won't fly, because the pull would drag the flames out over the rocks and leave him dark.
What you count in the wilds
Wisps let go. A beaten wisp in the wilds does not die. Its light comes loose and drifts home toward the fair's glow on the horizon (painted in W4 and F1). Same 3, 4, 5 rule as A. The lamplighter's lantern at W4 shows the count: its flame leans toward the crag at first and stands straighter with each one let go. Zone 3 opens at twelve: the call is thin enough that the captain's lamps burn straight, so he hangs all twelve and flies.
The great wraith
She lies coiled in the cold cradle round every light that answered her over the years. Those are the flames in her ribs and the lanterns on her chain. The wisps strung across the moor were her reach toward the fair.
Why the four go
Letting the wisps go only thins the call for one night. While she sits in the cradle it will pull again tomorrow, at the fair's candles and the captain's lamps.
The ending
When she falls she does not vanish. Her flames and her lanterns' lights pour into the cradle and catch, and the beacon burns warm again, its old fire given back its hearth. The wisps still on the stair rise into it. Io's line already written fits: 'It isn't ours. Let it go where it belongs.'
What it shows off
The fair as the brightest thing this country sees once in a lifetime, which is why it all happens tonight. Also the wisps' sad faces, and Io and the Jester as people who mend rather than just win.
Leans on
What the wraiths are: that wisps are cold flames and the great wraith is the beacon's own fire.
Its weakest point
The call is felt only through leaning flames, so the count is less solid in the hand than twelve lamps. Fighting wisps in order to free them needs one clear line, such as 'they put out whatever they touch', or it feels odd.
What would change in what is made
  • No lamp prop; after a wilds win, a freed light drifts off toward the fair's glow
  • Rug candles at W1 and the lantern flame at W4 lean toward the crag; the W4 flame straightens as the count climbs
  • W3 opening scene rewritten: the captain's lamps sit in a crate (one small prop); the empty brackets now mean that
  • The hull lamps lighting one by one goes; at twelve he hangs them all at once, which fits W8
  • Lamplighter's and captain's lines rewritten around the pull
  • F5 ending: the cradle catches fire and burns
  • Great wraith: no change

No painting needs redoing.

D   The Fox sews the night shut medium to change

Something has cut the night open over the moor, and wisps slip through the cut like draughts through a torn tent. Only the Fox, who cuts and sews the fabric of the world, can see it. She sews it shut a stitch at a time, using the light of each wisp the four beat as her thread. The cut runs all the way to the crag, where the great wraith is holding it open.

At the fair
At dusk in the square the rug candles lean and the Fox's bell rings by itself. She says the evening has a draught in it. At the mooring field wisps pour in over the gate from one spot in the sky. The Fox sees a thin, ragged line in the night, running over the moor toward the crag. The captain has taken his lamps in and won't fly: 'I don't take her into a sky that's coming apart.'
What you count in the wilds
Stitches. After each wilds win the Fox pulls the beaten wisp's light thin and sews it in as one stitch. Same 3, 4, 5 rule as A. A cold blue line of stitches grows across the night sky in W4 to W6 and F1. Zone 3 opens at the twelfth stitch: the cut is closed across the moor, and the last open stretch hangs in the sky over the crag, which only the airship can reach.
The great wraith
At the top of the beacon she has her long hands in the cut, holding it open. The flames in her ribs are light from whatever lies on the other side.
Why the four go
In the Fox's words: a seam that isn't tied off isn't a seam. By morning it would unpick itself.
The ending
She falls. The others hold the edges together while the Fox puts the last stitch through, snips with her scissors, and her bell rings once. The blue thread glows and fades, the flames in the wraith's ribs go out as the night closes, and Auros is where it has been all evening.
What it shows off
The Fox's fabric magic, her bell, scissors and cold blue foxfire. It is a story about one of the four rather than about the captain.
Leans on
Where wraiths come from (what is on the other side of the cut), how far the Fox's magic reaches, and who made the cut.
Its weakest point
Magic fixing magic is hard to feel. The cut has to be drawn well over the paintings or the player sees nothing. The other three play second fiddle. And it raises a big question, what is on the other side, that the demo can't answer.
What would change in what is made
  • No lamp prop; a cold blue stitched line drawn over the night skies of W4 to W6 and F1, one stitch per win
  • W1: new moment, the Fox's bell rings by itself
  • W3 opening scene rewritten: wisps pour in from one spot in the sky; the hull lamps lighting one by one goes
  • A short sewing moment for the Fox after each wilds win
  • F5 ending: the last stitch over the cradle
  • Great wraith: look kept; you could change the glow colour

No painting needs redoing.

Opus would pick C. One idea answers both of the mapper's open questions. Wisps are flames answering a call, and the fair, the brightest light here in a lifetime, explains why it happens tonight. The stake is still alive at the top of the stair, because the call is still there after the twelfth wisp is let go. It uses lines already written (candles leaning with no wind, the lamplighter who won't leave her lantern, Io's 'let it go where it belongs'), makes the wisps' sad faces mean something, and costs little with no repaint.

What could be joined: A and C fit together well. Keep A's twelve lamps as the count, since W3, W8 and the counting rule are built for them. Put C's reason underneath: the lamps were pulled toward a cold hearth, not stolen. Then choose A's ending (the light goes home and the beacon stays dark, as W9 is painted) or C's (the beacon burns again). B's crystal heart could be what lies cold in the cradle in C. The Fox's stitching from D could be a small moment for her at the end of any of them.

Its questions for you:

  1. Are the wisps villains, or sad lights that can be set free?
  2. At the end, should the beacon burn, or stay dark as you painted it?
  3. Do you want the demo to show crystal power at work, or keep it in the background?
  4. Should the story be the captain's problem, or something that reaches the four themselves?

The two kinds of fight picture

When a fight starts, the 3D witches and foes stand on a painting. The game's camera has to look at them from the same place the painter looked at the ground, or their feet will not sit on it. The borrowed Envoi pictures come in two kinds, and the mapper used both.

Both of these show the same Envoi place, the dead moonwell, which is drafted for the lamp room.

What the question is: may some fights be seen level and others from above? If yes, the fight camera changes from place to place, each kind needs its own tuning, and the witches' moves are seen from a different side in different fights.

What I would do: keep every fight seen level, like your own painting. Every fight test so far has used that view, it shows the fighters larger (you asked for a closer fight camera), and there is one fight camera to get right. Envoi has a level picture of the same place for the lamp room and for the crag, so those two can simply be swapped. Only the fair has no level picture, and it was a poor fit anyway: it wants a painting of its own.

The evening, beat by beat (the lamp story, as first drafted)

  1. At dusk the four witches are at home in the fair square, among people who know them.
  2. Wisps drift in after the fair's lights, and the four see them off in the square and the stall row.
  3. At the mooring field they arrive as wisps carry the twelve lamps of the captain's airship out over the gate, and he will not fly her dark.
  4. They go out onto the moor at night and win the first lamps back at the Last Lantern.
  5. A Shadow Wraith bars the road at the standing stones, and they break through.
  6. At the still pool they find a camp to rest at and win the last lamps; a hollow off the path hides a healing amulet.
  7. With all twelve lit on the hull, the captain flies them to a dead airship beacon on a crag.
  8. In deep night they climb the beacon stair.
  9. In the lamp room at the top a great wraith hoards the stolen light, and they take it back.

Zone 1: The Moon Faire

W1   The fair square dusk

In use: your painting

The existing painting: a ring of worn cobbles round packed earth, with a red rug edged in candles at its centre, a roofed stone well to the right, and paths leaving left, right and near. Round it stand a red-and-cream striped round tent and a gold tent (far left), two awning stalls of bottles and cloth (far), a blue star-patterned tent (far right), a basket stall and a green-and-gold tent (right), a lamp stall and a blue moon-painted wagon (near left), crates and barrels (near right) and about eight lit lamp posts; I see no bunting. The sky band is violet dusk with pink on the horizon, low hills and far tent tops, and Auros full in the upper left.

Ways out: right to W2 (the path between the basket stall and the green-and-gold tent)

Who is here

Lamp-seller at the lamp stall on the near left, beside the blue wagon; sits on a stool behind the counter trimming wicks; beckons when the party comes near
“Evening, you four. Come and look, looking's free.”
“I've sold lamps since I could count change. Never once saw a light get up and leave.”
“Take this wick out to the lamplighter, would you? Last lantern on the road.”
Ribbon Dyer under the far awning hung with cloth; stands stirring a dye pot; greets with a bow, thinks before answering
“Blue is short tonight. The one with the fox ears had most of it.”
“Dusk is the best light for red. In an hour it's all one colour.”
Fortune-teller in the doorway of the blue star-patterned tent, far right; stands turning one card over and over; beckons
“One coin, one card. You travel with us and you've never once sat down.”
“A road, and something standing on it. That's all the card says.”
Ballad singer on the red rug in the middle of the ring, among its candles; stands singing; stops and bows when spoken to
“I'll do the long one when the lamps are all lit. People stay for the long one.”
“The candles keep leaning. There's no wind.”

Things that can happen

  • W1-a The rug candles gutter fight
    As the walking witch heads for the right-hand path, the candles on the rug dip and a single wisp drops over the well: the first set fight, one wisp, to teach turns. Jester: 'Oh good. I was getting bored.'
  • W1-b The blue wagon rest
    The moon-painted wagon is the party's own and the first rest spot: they wake here after any loss at the fair.
  • W1-c One coin, one card talk
    The fortune-teller turns a card and gives the one line about a road. Jester: 'It says that for everyone.' Io: 'Then everyone should mind the road.'
  • W1-d A wick for the lamplighter errand
    The lamp-seller asks the party to carry a trimmed wick to the lamplighter at the last lantern on the moor road. It ends at W4 with thanks and nothing else.

Fights: One set fight (a single wisp at the rug candles); no walking fights.

W2   The stall row and the sparring ring dusk

In use: your painting (November 13)

How the guide sits on your painting

The green lines are the guide: the walkable ground, the big shapes and the 1.70 m figure. Where they sit on the painted things, people will stand and walk where the painting says they should.

The guide itself, with labels (green: ways out; blue: where people stand):

A straight lane of trodden earth and straw running left to right between awning stalls and shuttered booths, opening midway on the far side onto a roped ring of sawdust with a lamp post at each corner. An oven cart stands at the left end and a pie cart at the right. The sky band is a shade deeper than W1, with tent tops and bare flag poles against it and Auros in the upper left.

Ways out: left to W1 (the lane back to the square), right to W3 (the end of the row, where the stalls stop and the field begins)

Who is here

Fair Baker at the oven cart, left end of the row; stands at the oven door; waves a floury hand, laughs easily
“Buns are just out. Mind, they're hot.”
“If they come for my oven they'll get the peel across the nose. Do they have noses?”
Old night-watchman at a corner post of the sparring ring; stands watching the four ring lamps; nods, points at the ring
“Shutters first, then lamps. That's my round, and something's ahead of me tonight.”
“Knocked flat? You'll wake up by your wagon. No shame in it. Go again.”
Pie seller at her cart, right end of the row, on the way to the gate; stands behind the cart; waves, points at the pies
“Hot pies! Mutton, and the other one's mutton too.”
“That captain's had nothing since noon. Take him one, he's good for the coin.”

Things that can happen

  • W2-a Wisps at the ring lamps fight
    Two wisps circle the corner lamps of the ring; passing the ring mouth starts the second set fight. Fox: 'Two! One each and two to share.'
  • W2-b Practice bouts in the ring fight
    After W2-a the watchman waves the party into the ring whenever they like, to fight the wisps that keep drifting to its lamps. Bouts repeat, give no lamps and cost nothing to lose.
  • W2-c A pie for the captain errand
    The pie-seller sends a pie to the mooring field; the captain's thanks ('Mutton. Good woman.') ends it. Ranger: 'I'm carrying it. You three would eat it.'
  • W2-d The watchman's advice talk
    Talking to the watchman after a first loss or first bout gives his line about waking by the wagon, so the rule is told by a person and not a screen.

Fights: One set fight (two wisps at the ring lamps) and repeatable practice bouts in the ring; no walking fights.

W3   The mooring field dusk

In use: your painting (November 13)

How the guide sits on your painting

The green lines are the guide: the walkable ground, the big shapes and the 1.70 m figure. Where they sit on the painted things, people will stand and walk where the painting says they should.

The guide itself, with labels (green: ways out; blue: where people stand):

Trampled grass at the edge of the fair, with the last tent backs on the left and the fair gate on the right (two poles, a bar, a coin table and a brazier), where the road runs out into darkening heather. The captain's airship is moored along the far side, with a ladder down to two mooring posts and twelve lamp brackets along the hull. The sky band holds the last red of dusk under violet, the ship's rigging dark against it, and Auros in the upper left.

Ways out: left to W2 (back into the stall row), right to W4 (out under the gate bar onto the moor road), far to W8 (up the ship's ladder; the captain flies them once all twelve lamps are lit)

Who is here

Gate keeper at the coin table by the gate bar; stands with arms folded watching the moor road; points, looks cross
“Out is free. Back in after dark, I look at your face first.”
“Twelve lights went over my gate and not one paid. I counted.”
Chestnut roaster at the brazier just inside the gate; stands turning chestnuts; beckons and laughs
“Here, a handful for the road. No, put your purse away.”
“Went straight over my head, the lot of them. Nearly had my hat.”
The captain at the foot of the ship's ladder, between the mooring posts; walks from post to post looking up at the dark hull; turns to the party when spoken to
“Twelve lamps, and they lifted every one like fruit off a branch.”
“I don't take her up dark. Bring my lamps home and I'll fly you wherever you point.”

Things that can happen

  • W3-a Twelve lamps go little scene
    On first entering, the party sees the last lit lamps lift off the hull and stream over the gate toward the moor, each carried by a wisp. The captain runs to the ladder too late.
    Needs: the captain's model; the airship with twelve lamps that can be lit or dark; a lamp a wisp can be seen carrying
  • W3-b Stragglers at the mooring ropes fight
    Three wisps that stayed behind at the mooring posts: the third set fight. Io: 'Keep them off the ropes.' Jester: 'Keep them on me.'
  • W3-c The captain asks talk
    After W3-b the captain tells the four the lamps went out over the moor and asks for them back; the gate-keeper's line about counting twelve backs him up. Nothing bars the gate.
    Needs: the captain's model and picture card
  • W3-d The lamps come home little scene
    Each time the party returns, the brackets on the hull light to match the lamps won so far, and the captain has a new line.
    Needs: the airship's lamps lighting one by one
  • W3-e All twelve lit gate
    With the twelfth lamp lit the captain lowers the ladder; talking to him flies the party to the landing ledge. This is the plan's gate to zone 3.
    Needs: a short flight cut or a fade; the maker's choice

Fights: One set fight (three wisps at the mooring ropes); no walking fights.

Ways out: left to W4 (the track back down to the Last Lantern), right to W6 (the road between the two tallest stones, shut until the Shadow Wraith is beaten), near to W7 (a gap in the gorse behind the fallen stone, easy to miss)

Things that can happen

  • W5-a A word before the stones little scene
    On arriving the party sees the shape standing in the road. Io: 'That is no wisp.' Jester: 'No. That one's mine.'
  • W5-b The wraith on the road fight
    A Shadow Wraith stands between the two tallest stones and the road beyond stays shut until it is beaten: the set fight. Winning brings back a lamp.
    Needs: the F3 backdrop
  • W5-c Lamps among the stones fight
    Walking fights round the ring against wisps, later with a Shadow Wraith among them; three wins bring back this area's other three lamps.
  • W5-d The gap behind the fallen stone find
    A narrow way down through the gorse on the near side leads to the hollow. Nothing marks it but a faint shine below.
    Needs: a small glow at the gap

Fights: The set fight against the Shadow Wraith that bars the road, and walking fights about every 14 metres. Lamps won here: 4.

W6   The still pool and the broken arch night

In use: your painting (November 13)

How the guide sits on your painting

The green lines are the guide: the walkable ground, the big shapes and the 1.70 m figure. Where they sit on the painted things, people will stand and walk where the painting says they should.

The guide itself, with labels (green: ways out; blue: where people stand):

The track runs down to a round black pool lying dead still, with a dry shelf of turf on the near bank holding a fire ring, a log seat and a bundle of cut rushes. On the far bank stands a broken stone arch, one leg upright and the span fallen in the reeds. The sky band is night with stars, and Auros in the upper left shows a second time in the water.

Ways out: left to W5 (the track back up to the stones)

Who is here

Farm lad on the log by the camp fire; sits feeding the fire; jumps up and waves. Met beyond the fair because he came out by day to cut rushes for the ponies' bedding and would not walk back past the wraith on the road.
“You came past the stones? Past that thing? I've been sat here since it sat there.”
“Came out for rushes for the ponies' beds. Got the rushes. Can't say much else for the day.”
“There's a dip back by the stones, behind the one that's fallen. Something shines down there. I didn't go and look.”

Things that can happen

  • W6-a The camp by the pool rest
    The fire and the log are the plan's rest spot: the party rests here and wakes here after a loss on the moor. Fox: 'A fire nobody stole. Lovely.'
    Needs: a fire prop and a log seat
  • W6-b Under the broken arch fight
    A Shadow Wraith and two wisps hold lamps under the arch on the far bank: the set fight. Winning brings back a lamp.
  • W6-c The last lamps fight
    Walking fights round the bank; four wins bring back this area's other four lamps.
  • W6-d What the farm lad saw talk
    His third line points the party back to the fallen stone at W5 and the hollow below it.
  • W6-e Twelve in hand little scene
    When the twelfth lamp is won, most likely here, the Ranger says: 'That's twelve. Back to the ship.' Jester: 'And then wherever they were taking them.'

Fights: One set fight under the broken arch and walking fights about every 14 metres. Lamps won here: 5.

W7   The hollow night

In use: your painting (November 13)

How the guide sits on your painting

The green lines are the guide: the walkable ground, the big shapes and the 1.70 m figure. Where they sit on the painted things, people will stand and walk where the painting says they should.

The guide itself, with labels (green: ways out; blue: where people stand):

A steep-sided dip below the stones, floored with moss and bracken, with a flat grey stone at its middle and a thread of water beside it. Rock and gorse close it in on every side but the far one, where the way climbs back. The sky band is narrow above the rim, with stars and Auros in the upper left.

Ways out: far to W5 (the climb back through the gorse to the fallen stone)

Things that can happen

  • W7-a Down out of the wind little scene
    On entering, the Fox says: 'Oh, I like it down here. Nobody tell anybody.'
  • W7-b The amulet on the flat stone find
    The plan's healing amulet lies on the flat stone, giving off the faint shine seen from above. Io: 'It mends. I'll carry it.'
    Needs: an amulet prop; what it does is the maker's
  • W7-c Wisps follow them down fight
    Walking fights happen here as on the rest of the moor but bring no lamps, only practice.

Fights: Walking fights about every 14 metres as in the rest of the wilds; no set fight and no lamps.

Zone 3: The Dark Beacon

W8   The landing ledge deep night

In use: your painting (November 13)

How the guide sits on your painting

The green lines are the guide: the walkable ground, the big shapes and the 1.70 m figure. Where they sit on the painted things, people will stand and walk where the painting says they should.

The guide itself, with labels (green: ways out; blue: where people stand):

A narrow shelf of bare rock on the side of the crag, with the airship lying along its near edge and all twelve lamps lit, the only warm light in the picture. At the right the first worn steps of a stair are cut up into the rock, and the dead tower stands above as a black shape. The sky band is deep night, thick with stars, with Auros in the upper left.

Ways out: near to W3 (aboard the airship; the captain flies them back to the mooring field), right to W9 (the foot of the stair)

Who is here

The captain at the ship's ladder on the near edge of the ledge; stands with one hand on the ladder, looking up at the tower; turns to the party when spoken to
“This ledge is as near as I can lay her. The rest is stairs.”
“I'll keep all twelve burning. Look down if you lose heart.”
“Rest aboard whenever you like. I'm going nowhere without you.”

Things that can happen

  • W8-a Setting down on the ledge little scene
    The arrival: the ship comes alongside and the four step off into the dark. Io: 'No light at the top. None at all.' Jester: 'Then we'll bring some.'
    Needs: the captain's model; the airship with all twelve lamps lit
  • W8-b Rest aboard rest
    A rest spot at the ladder: a loss on the stair or in the lamp room wakes the party here and not back at the pool.
  • W8-c Back to the fair talk
    Talking to the captain flies the party back to the mooring field, for the ring or anything left undone.
  • W8-d The first step little scene
    At the foot of the stair the Ranger says: 'I'll count the steps.' Fox: 'Count them on the way down. It's more cheerful.'

Fights: none

W9   The beacon stair deep night

In use: your painting (November 13)

How the guide sits on your painting

The green lines are the guide: the walkable ground, the big shapes and the 1.70 m figure. Where they sit on the painted things, people will stand and walk where the painting says they should.

The guide itself, with labels (green: ways out; blue: where people stand):

Worn stone steps climbing the crag and then winding round the outside of the tower, with small landings and rusted lamp brackets on the wall, every one empty. One landing gives onto a side ledge round the back of the tower, and the stair ends at a shut door. The sky band is deep night, open and starry on the outer side, with Auros in the upper left and the ship's twelve lamps small and warm far below.

Ways out: left to W8 (down the stair to the landing ledge), far to F5 (the door at the top of the stair, which opens at level 5)

Things that can happen

  • W9-a Wraiths on the stair fight
    Walking fights up the steps and landings against Shadow Wraiths with wisps.
    Needs: the F4 backdrop
  • W9-b The charm on the side ledge find
    Off one landing, round the back of the tower, the plan's charm hangs from an empty lamp bracket. Ranger: 'Somebody climbed all this way to hang that up.'
    Needs: a charm prop; what it does is the maker's
  • W9-c The door at the top gate
    The lamp-room door stays shut until the party is level 5; before that the Ranger says 'Not yet. We're not ready.' This is the plan's level gate.
  • W9-d The ship below little scene
    On the top landing the twelve lamps show far below. Io: 'He kept them lit.' Jester: 'He'd better. We paid for them.'
    Needs: the lit ship painted small into the view

Fights: Walking fights about every 14 metres against Shadow Wraiths and wisps; no set fight.

F5   The lamp room deep night

A fight place: no walking picture.

To be painted: a round stone floor at the top of the tower, walled by a ring of tall broken window arches open to the night. In the middle stands a stepped stone cradle where the beacon's lamp should burn, cold and dark; how the hoarded light shows is the maker's to decide. Through the arches the sky band is deep night and stars, with Auros in the upper left where it has been all evening.

Ways out: near to W9 (the door back onto the top landing)

Things that can happen

  • F5-a A word at the door little scene
    Before the fight the Jester says: 'Stay behind me. I mean it this time.' Fox: 'You always mean it.' Jester: 'This time I'll do it.'
  • F5-b The great wraith fight
    The plan's last set fight: the great wraith, two Shadow Wraiths and two wisps. Losing wakes the party at the last rest spot.
    Needs: the F5 backdrop
  • F5-c The light let go little scene
    When the great wraith falls, the stolen light comes loose in the room. Io: 'It isn't ours. Let it go where it belongs.'
    Needs: a light effect, and the maker's word on where the light goes
  • F5-d Down to the ship little scene
    The demo's last moment: the walking witch goes back out onto the landing with the twelve lamps below. Fox: 'Race you down.' Ranger: 'No.'
    Needs: an end card or fade

Fights: The great wraith with two Shadow Wraiths and two wisps, behind the door that opens at level 5.

The captain

W3: “Twelve lamps, and they lifted every one like fruit off a branch.” “I don't take her up dark. Bring my lamps home and I'll fly you wherever you point.” “Every one of them went the same way. Out past the stones, toward the old beacon.”

W8: “This ledge is as near as I can lay her. The rest is stairs.” “I'll keep all twelve burning. Look down if you lose heart.” “Rest aboard whenever you like. I'm going nowhere without you.”

His model is being built in another session.

Backgrounds in use now

Still needed

  • The captain's 3D model and picture card. He speaks in two areas and opens the way to zone 3. (W3, W8)
  • The airship as a moored set piece with twelve lamps that light one at a time. The lamp count is shown on the hull, and the lit ship is the only warm light at the beacon. (W3, W8, W9)
  • The maker's own battle paintings for the fair and the lamp room, and ideally the crag. Nothing borrowed shows a tented fair, a tower-top room or a stair on a crag, so F2, F4 and F5 are stand-ins only. (W1, W2, W3, W9, F5)
  • A ship's lamp a wisp can be seen carrying, and a short 'lamp won' sound and line. The theft at the field and each lamp's return need to be seen and heard. (W3, W4, W5, W6)
  • Small props: stools and a log to sit on, a dye pot with steam, oven cart, pie cart, brazier, coin table and gate bar, ring ropes, camp fire, amulet, charm. People need something to stand at or sit on, and the two finds need something to pick up. (W1, W2, W3, W6, W7, W9)
  • A short sung tune for the ballad-singer. She is drafted as singing on the rug until spoken to. (W1)
  • Picture cards for the eleven fair folk and the four witches, if not already made. Every talk shows a card beside the text box. (all)
